name: Renaissance Periodization (RP) volume training
lead: Renaissance Periodization (RP) is a fitness company co-founded in 2012 by Mike Israetel and Nick Shaw [1][2]. It is associated with a volume-management framework for muscle building built around three weekly set benchmarks: minimum effective volume (MEV), maximum adaptive volume (MAV) and maximum recoverable volume (MRV) [2].

Israetel is an American exercise scientist and bodybuilder with a PhD in sports physiology [1]. RP offers coaching, apps, courses and ebooks, and the volume landmarks are popular in lifting communities as a way to plan how many sets to do per muscle each week [2].
No independent trials of the RP system as a whole were identified in the sources consulted, and one encyclopedic source states that no large-scale independent efficacy studies were found [2].
infobox: 2012, by Mike Israetel and Nick Shaw [1][2]
Coaching, hypertrophy and diet apps, courses, ebooks [2]

paras: MEV is the lowest weekly volume that produces growth, MAV is the range where adaptation is described as best, and MRV is the most volume a person can recover from. Trainees are advised in RP materials to start low and add sets according to recovery. Published figures in one summary give MRV ranges of roughly 12-26 sets per week for smaller muscles and 20-30 or more for larger ones, with beginners starting near maintenance [2]. Those figures come from an AI-generated summary and from RP's own materials rather than from independent trials.

RP began from Israetel's online content and grew into a team offering one-on-one coaching, the RP Hypertrophy App and Diet Coach App, courses and ebooks, a YouTube channel and a podcast [2]. The company does not sell its own supplement line, according to the same summary [2].

The summary cites research on training frequency, periodization and repetitions in reserve, and notes that RP-affiliated authors co-wrote a 2022 paper on load progression and muscle size and that RP partly funded a 2019 study on high-volume training [2]. Muscle-hypertrophy reviews describe volume, intensity and frequency as variables that influence growth [3].

Critics cited in the same summary say some of the carbohydrate recommendations are high for most people, that templates and subscriptions are costly, and that claims may be overhyped relative to other evidence-based approaches [2]. In September 2025 a video criticised Israetel's doctoral dissertation, and he said he had uploaded the wrong draft and released a corrected version [1].
No studies found testing the RP volume-landmark system as a whole. Broader research on training volume exists [3].

timeline.event: Israetel and Nick Shaw co-found Renaissance Periodization [1][2].
Israetel competes in bodybuilding for the first time [1].
A video criticises errors in Israetel's dissertation; a corrected version is released [1].

lore.intro: RP volume landmarks are commonly cited in lifting communities as a way to decide weekly set counts.

claims.claim: Each muscle has a personal range of weekly sets (MEV to MRV) that should guide programming.
claims.believers: Followers say tracking these landmarks helps them add volume gradually and deload before overreaching [2].
claims.experts: Hypertrophy reviews describe volume as influencing growth [3], but the sources consulted report no independent trial validating the specific landmark ranges.

card.summary: Israetel's MEV/MAV/MRV set-count framework: popular in lifting circles, with no independent trial of the system itself.
card.note: Figures come largely from RP's own and affiliated material.

quick.overview:
Renaissance Periodization is a coaching company founded in 2012 by Mike Israetel and Nick Shaw. Its best-known idea is a set of weekly volume landmarks: minimum effective, maximum adaptive and maximum recoverable volume.

The framework is widely discussed among lifters. Independent efficacy studies of the full system were not found.
quick.mechanism: Trainees begin at a low weekly set count per muscle and add sets over a training block as recovery allows, then reduce volume before repeating.
quick.risks: Higher volumes carry general overuse and fatigue risks of resistance training. Critics mention cost and some diet recommendations; no system-specific harm data were identified.
